title: Postoperative Urinary Retention -- Continuing Education Activity
content: Postoperative urinary retention is the inability to urinate after a surgical procedure despite having a full bladder in patients without a prior history of urinary disorders. This complication is relatively common in both outpatient and inpatient settings, with multiple potential etiologies. Delayed recognition and treatment of postoperative urinary retention can contribute to significant postoperative morbidity, including prolonged hospitalization and development of urinary tract infections, detrusor dysfunction, overflow incontinence, pain crisis, and renal failure in severe cases.

title: Postoperative Urinary Retention -- Continuing Education Activity
content: Inappropriate urethral catheterization in patients misdiagnosed with postoperative urinary retention may lead to unnecessary distress, urethral trauma, hematuria, bladder injury, catheter blockage, stricture formation, and other urethral catheter-associated complications. Therefore, the ability to assess, recognize, and appropriately manage postoperative urinary retention is essential for any healthcare provider responsible for treating a postoperative patient. Initial management typically involves urethral or Foley catheterization; however, selected cases may require further evaluation and additional therapeutic interventions.

title: Postoperative Urinary Retention -- Introduction
content: Postoperative urinary retention (POUR) is the inability to urinate after a surgical procedure despite having a full bladder. [1] [2] This condition can cause significant physical and emotional distress to some patients or remain unnoticed in asymptomatic patients. Although often easily reversible with minimal intervention, POUR can result in substantial long-term morbidity if unrecognized or managed inappropriately. Delayed recognition and treatment of POUR contribute to significant postoperative morbidity, including prolonged hospitalization and development of urinary tract infections, detrusor damage from overdistension, voiding dysfunction, overflow incontinence, pain, vesicoureteral reflux, inappropriate or accidental catheter extraction, and renal failure in severe cases. [2] [3] [4] [5] [6] [7]

content: The reported prevalence of POUR ranges from 5% to 70% due to a lack of a standardized definition; regardless, it is not uncommon in hospitals, emergency departments, or clinical settings. [3] Accurate recognition and appropriate management of POUR are essential for healthcare providers responsible for postoperative patients. [1] [2] [3]

title: Postoperative Urinary Retention -- Etiology
content: Normal bladder function depends on coordination between the somatic and autonomic nervous systems. [9] [10] [11] [12] There are generally 2 stages of urination—filling (storage) and active voiding. [9] [12] During the filling (storage) stage, the sympathetic innervation of the bladder derived from the thoracolumbar spinal cord (T10 to L2) inhibits the detrusor muscle of the bladder while stimulating (activating) the bladder neck, base, and prostatic urethra. [9] [10] [11] [12] Meanwhile, the external sphincter is constricted via the somatic-pudendal nerve (S2-4). [9] [10] [11] [12] [13]

title: Postoperative Urinary Retention -- Etiology
content: During the emptying stage, parasympathetic innervation of the bladder, derived from the pelvic nerves (S2-S4), activates the detrusor muscle while relaxing the bladder neck and urethral smooth muscle. [9] [10] [11] [12] At the same time, the somatic or volitional nervous system relaxes the external urethral sphincter via the pudendal nerve, thereby providing voluntary control over urination. [9] [10] [11] [12] [13]

title: Postoperative Urinary Retention -- Etiology
content: POUR generally arises from a combination of decreased neurological signaling, reduced bladder sensation, diminished detrusor contractility, mechanical obstruction, prolonged effect of anesthetic drugs, and bladder muscle dysfunction or injury from overdistension. [14] These factors contribute to increased postoperative pain, bladder muscle damage, increased risk of urinary tract infections, prolonged hospitalization, higher healthcare costs, and delayed rehabilitation. [14] Overstretching of the smooth muscle fibers of the bladder from overdistension not only causes physical damage but also results in intramural ischemia, nerve damage, ischemic muscle injury, and loss of bladder tone. [15] [16] High intravesical pressure, if severe or prolonged, can result in vesicoureteral reflux. [17] Due to the complexity of the urination signalling pathway, there are many perioperative risk factors for POUR, which can be categorized into patient, procedure, anesthetic, and postoperative factors.

title: Postoperative Urinary Retention -- Etiology -- Patient Characteristics
content: Patient characteristics that increase the risk of POUR include male sex, older age, smaller maximum bladder capacity, regular anticholinergic or opioid use, history of pelvic surgery, benign prostatic hyperplasia, urinary tract infections, neurological pathologies, hypertension, and diabetes mellitus. [2] [18] [19] [20] [21] Because individual characteristics vary, it is helpful for patients to measure their maximum voluntary bladder capacity at home and use this volume as the upper limit when performing postoperative bladder ultrasonography to assess residual volume. [18]

title: Postoperative Urinary Retention -- Etiology -- Patient Characteristics
content: POUR is more common in men (4.7%) than women (2.9%), due to anatomical and prostatic enlargement factors. The risk increases approximately 2.4-fold with advancing age, beginning in patients older than 50, most likely due to detrusor damage and dysfunction over time, as well as progressive degenerative neuronal factors. [2] [22] [23] [24]

title: Postoperative Urinary Retention -- Etiology -- Procedural Factors
content: Procedural factors associated with a higher risk of POUR include the type and duration of surgery, with longer operative times and procedures such as joint arthroplasty, anorectal surgery, hernia repair, spinal procedures, and gynecological surgery. [2] [18] [19] [20] For example, up to 43% of orthopedic patients suffer from POUR. [14]

title: Postoperative Urinary Retention -- Etiology -- Anesthesia Factors
content: Anesthesia factors increasing the risk of POUR include the use of spinal anaesthesia, higher doses of opioids, longer-acting anesthetic medications, the use of glycopyrrolate, and greater volumes of intraoperative intravenous fluids. [2] [18] [25] Postoperative contributing factors include prolonged epidural analgesia, increased opioid use, delayed time to ambulation, and ileus. [2] [18]

title: Postoperative Urinary Retention -- Etiology -- Anesthesia Factors
content: Undergoing surgery and anesthesia alters the complex urinary signaling pathway in multiple ways, which tips patients with pre-disposing risk factors over a certain threshold into urinary retention post-operatively. Anesthesia can pharmacologically impact normal micturition. General, spinal, and regional anesthetics can all lead to POUR by suppressing micturition control and reflexes at both the central nervous system (the pontine micturition center) and the peripheral nervous system, by blocking neural transmission in the sacral spinal cord. [26] [27] General anesthetic agents act as smooth muscle relaxants, decreasing bladder contractility while interfering with the autonomic regulation of the detrusor. [28] The effect is more pronounced in longer surgeries, especially those lasting longer than 4 hours. [2] The significant increase in bladder capacity observed during general anesthesia clearly supports this finding. [28]

title: Postoperative Urinary Retention -- Etiology -- Anesthesia Factors
content: Spinal and epidural anesthetic agents affect voiding through a distinct mechanism by effectively interfering with the pelvic afferent and efferent nerves and the micturition reflex arcs as they enter and exit the spinal cord and ascend to the central micturition centers. [26] [28] Spinal anesthesia eliminates the sensory perception of bladder fullness. [26] Hourly urine production tends to be greater, and recovery of normal bladder function is slower with spinal than with general anesthesia. [18]

title: Postoperative Urinary Retention -- Etiology -- Anesthesia Factors
content: Neuromuscular blocking agents administered during surgery are reversed with anticholinesterases, such as neostigmine, which often require concurrent administration of an anticholinergic agent, such as glycopyrrolate, to regulate muscarinic overactivity. [25] [29] [30] Glycopyrrolate use is associated with an increased incidence of POUR. [25] [30] In contrast, sugammadex, a reversal agent, does not require anticholinergic coadministration and can reduce the incidence of POUR by about 50%. [25] [31] [32] [33] [34] [35] [36] However, despite its clinical advantages, the substantially higher cost of sugammadex compared with traditional agents such as neostigmine limits its routine use. [33] [36] [37]

title: Postoperative Urinary Retention -- Etiology -- Perioperative Medications
content: Perioperative medications may also play a role in the development of POUR. Opioids, in particular, decrease the sensation of bladder distension by inhibiting bladder sensory parasympathetics while also increasing bladder neck tone through sympathetic overstimulation, leading to an increase in outlet obstruction. [38] Surgical pain, via activation of the sympathetic nervous system, leads to detrusor relaxation and bladder neck contraction—essentially a constant bladder filling and storage effect. [28] [39]

title: Postoperative Urinary Retention -- Etiology -- Perioperative Medications
content: Finally, the destruction or alteration of part of the anatomy vital to voiding can also lead to POUR. Pelvic surgeries, in particular, place the autonomic nervous system and pelvic plexi at risk, which has led to significant efforts being made to embrace nerve-sparing procedures when possible. [40]

title: Postoperative Urinary Retention -- Epidemiology
content: Reported rates of POUR vary significantly in the literature, ranging from 5% to 70%. [2] [18] This broad variability is potentially due to the lack of a standardized definition of POUR across studies. [1] In addition, due to the multifactorial nature of POUR and significant variations in procedures and anesthetic use across and within surgical specialties, it is difficult to provide a universal incidence rate.

title: Postoperative Urinary Retention -- Epidemiology
content: Estimated rates of POUR differ by surgical category. Patients undergoing outpatient general surgical procedures develop POUR at a rate of 3.8%. [41] Patients undergoing outpatient orthopedic procedures have been found to develop POUR at a rate of between 10% and 84%. [42] Anorectal surgery appears to lead to POUR at anywhere between 1% and 52%, whereas the rate after herniorrhaphy is between 5.9% and 38%. [39] [43]

title: Postoperative Urinary Retention -- History and Physical
content: Following a surgical procedure, POUR may present as suprapubic pain or discomfort, bladder spasm, and/or urine leaking combined with the inability to urinate. However, some or all of these symptoms may be disguised by anesthesia or sedation from the operation. [44] Several studies have demonstrated that 33% to 61% of outpatient surgical patients experienced no subjective symptoms of retention despite having a bladder volume exceeding the normal maximum of 500 mL. [45] [46] [47]

title: Postoperative Urinary Retention -- History and Physical
content: The average bladder filling rate is estimated at 100 mL/h during general anesthesia and about 170 mL/h during spinal anesthesia. [18] A bladder can be damaged if overdistended (filled beyond its normal maximum capacity) for more than just 2 to 3 hours. [18] [48] The time since the patient's last micturition should be noted, as most patients should not go more than 6 to 7 hours without urinating.

title: Postoperative Urinary Retention -- History and Physical
content: Physical examination should include palpation and percussion of the suprapubic area to assess for bladder fullness. Bladder fullness may present as suprapubic tension on palpation with associated dullness to percussion. The average bladder holds a maximum of around 500 mL, which, on physical examination, produces dullness to percussion in the suprapubic area just below the umbilicus. Dullness extending above the umbilicus may represent more than 1000 mL. [44] However, physical examination alone is relatively unreliable for estimating bladder volume. Noninvasive bedside ultrasound is widely available and provides a more accurate assessment. [2] [45] [49] [50]

title: Postoperative Urinary Retention -- Evaluation
content: If urinary issues were significant before surgery, a basic metabolic panel should be obtained preoperatively to identify any underlying renal disease from chronic retention. Given its ubiquity in the hospital setting, bedside ultrasonography for bladder residual urine determination (a bladder scanner) should be considered an extension of the physical examination in the recovery room to identify early POUR. [49] Several studies have demonstrated the accuracy of ultrasound-based volume measurements when compared to catheterization, and the technology continues to improve. [45] [49] However, accuracy deteriorates with extreme patient obesity and the presence of abdominal fluid, ascites, bowel obstruction, ovarian cysts, pelvic masses, severe pelvic organ prolapse (stage III/IV), or uterine fibroids. [49] [51] [52] [53] [54] [55] [56] [57] [58] Poor operator technique, scanner calibration problems, and device malfunctions may also cause errors. [49]

title: Postoperative Urinary Retention -- Evaluation
content: Bedside ultrasonography provides a rapid, noninvasive, painless, and accurate assessment of residual bladder urine volume, even in patients without overt signs or symptoms of POUR. [2] [6] [44] [49] [59] This modality also permits the reliable and objective evaluation of patients for POUR whose symptoms are suppressed by regional anesthesia; comorbidities, such as stroke and spinal cord injury; persistent postoperative sedation; opioid effects; or communication difficulties. [2] [44]

title: Postoperative Urinary Retention -- Evaluation
content: Clinical evaluation alone tends to underestimate bladder volume compared to ultrasonography. [2] Patients after surgery may not have a normal sensation of bladder filling and/or decreased ability to communicate. [2] In one study, 61% of patients after general anesthesia failed to report any bladder issues despite a measured bladder volume of over 600 mL. In contrast, other studies have indicated that at least 25% of postoperative patients develop POUR without demonstrating any symptoms. [2] [46] [47] [50]

In contrast, other studies have indicated that at least 25% of postoperative patients develop POUR without demonstrating any symptoms. [2] [46] [47] [50]

title: Postoperative Urinary Retention -- Evaluation
content: In general, patients are expected to void within 6 to 8 hours after Foley removal or within 3 hours after the end of surgery. [18] [60] Patients who have not voided within these parameters should be evaluated by bedside ultrasonography for possible bladder overdistension and urinary retention.

title: Postoperative Urinary Retention -- Evaluation
content: A bladder scan to measure residual volume should be routinely performed in all patients who have undergone long surgical procedures (≥4 hours) without a Foley catheter, and in all postoperative patients on arrival in the postoperative recovery room, as part of routine care. The scan should be repeated for patients who have not voided before discharge from the recovery room to identify those at risk for POUR and to permit timely intervention, such as catheterization, before excessive bladder overdistension and injury occur.

title: Postoperative Urinary Retention -- Treatment / Management -- Prevention of Postoperative Urinary Retention
content: Prevention is the most effective strategy for managing POUR and requires a multidisciplinary approach that involves identifying and optimizing preoperative, intraoperative, and postoperative risk factors.

title: Postoperative Urinary Retention -- Treatment / Management -- Prevention of Postoperative Urinary Retention
content: Several clinical studies and meta-analyses have demonstrated the benefit of preoperative prophylactic alpha-blocker use, typically tamsulosin, in patients at the greatest risk of POUR. [2] [4] [61] [62] [63] [64] [65] [66] [67] [68] For optimal effect, patients should be started on such prophylactic medications at least 3 to 5 days before surgery and continued for several days after the procedure. [15] [69] Patients already on preoperative alpha-blockers are at lower risk of developing POUR; a systematic review reported a 60% reduction in the risk of POUR in these patients. [4]

title: Postoperative Urinary Retention -- Treatment / Management -- Prevention of Postoperative Urinary Retention
content: Preoperative: Patients at greatest risk of developing POUR should be identified preoperatively based on risk factors such as age, sex, comorbidities, and surgery type. In fact, these risk factors are reproducible enough to generate a receiver operating characteristic curve with a predictive accuracy of POUR with an area under the curve of 0.70. [70] Men are at nearly double the risk of developing POUR than women. [41] Increasing age raises the risk of POUR by 2.4 times in patients older than 50. [22] [23]
contents: Postoperative Urinary Retention -- Treatment / Management -- Prevention of Postoperative Urinary Retention. Preoperative: Patients at greatest risk of developing POUR should be identified preoperatively based on risk factors such as age, sex, comorbidities, and surgery type. In fact, these risk factors are reproducible enough to generate a receiver operating characteristic curve with a predictive accuracy of POUR with an area under the curve of 0.70. [70] Men are at nearly double the risk of developing POUR than women. [41] Increasing age raises the risk of POUR by 2.4 times in patients older than 50. [22] [23]

title: Postoperative Urinary Retention -- Treatment / Management -- Prevention of Postoperative Urinary Retention
content: Some comorbidities frequently associated with POUR include renal failure; diabetes mellitus, especially with diabetic complications; and psychiatric illness, including depression. [70] Patients with untreated or undertreated benign prostatic hyperplasia are also at increased risk. Voiding symptoms, such as urgency, frequency, and nocturia, as measured by a higher International Prostate Symptom Score, are associated with a greater risk of POUR. [4] Patients undergoing knee, hip, spine, or colon surgeries were also at higher risk of developing POUR. [70] Urging patients to void and measuring bladder residual fluid in the preoperative holding area before entering the operating room can help prevent large postoperative bladder volumes. [18]

title: Postoperative Urinary Retention -- Treatment / Management -- Prevention of Postoperative Urinary Retention
content: Intraoperative: Intraoperative risk factors for POUR include prolonged exposure to propofol or isoflurane. [71] [72] [73] Longer-acting spinal anesthetic agents such as bupivacaine and tetracaine cause a significant delay in bladder function recovery long after their sensory effects have dissipated. [18] [72]

title: Postoperative Urinary Retention -- Treatment / Management -- Prevention of Postoperative Urinary Retention
content: In one study, an operating time exceeding 2 hours was identified as a significant predictor of POUR. [74] Another study of patients undergoing total joint replacement found that the risk of POUR increased by 25% for every 15 minutes spent in the operating room. [75] An increased volume of administered intraoperative intravenous fluid is also associated with a higher rate of POUR when a catheter is not placed preoperatively, likely due to bladder wall distension and detrusor stretching during surgery. [45]

content: The use of sugammadex as the neuromuscular reversal agent, which does not require concomitant anticholinergic agents, has been shown to reduce the rate of POUR by approximately 50%. [25] [31] [32] In some cases, using an intraoperative Foley catheter or a quick straight urethral catheterization before removing the patient from the operating room after a lengthy case may be helpful. [50]

content: Postoperative: Postoperative risk factors for the development of POUR include a slow time to ambulation and systemic opioid use. One study demonstrated that early ambulation decreased the POUR rate from 52% to 19%. [76] Systemic opioids are a frequent modality of postoperative pain control and are given either intravenously or orally.

title: Postoperative Urinary Retention -- Treatment / Management -- Prevention of Postoperative Urinary Retention
content: In general surgery populations, POUR is directly related to the number of systemic opioids used postoperatively. [23] Acupuncture, early ambulation after surgery, and nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs have also been shown to reduce POUR. [81] An interesting nonpharmacological measure that showed a significant reduction in POUR in 126 men was the placement of a hot pack on the suprapubic area; however, this finding has not been replicated. [82]

title: Postoperative Urinary Retention -- Treatment / Management -- Management of Postoperative Urinary Retention
content: If POUR develops, the bladder must be drained immediately. There is some controversy in the literature regarding the placement of an indwelling Foley catheter versus managing urinary retention with intermittent self-catheterization. [3] Some institutions recommend intermittent self-catheterization whenever possible to reduce the risk of bacteriuria and theoretical infection. [42] In contrast, others emphasize the benefits of indwelling Foley catheterization, citing maximal decompression, detrusor rehabilitation, and enhanced bladder rest. They caution that intermittent catheterization may compromise bladder rest and result in intermittent overdistension, which has been shown to cause both acute and long-term detrusor decompensation. [42] [83]

title: Postoperative Urinary Retention -- Treatment / Management -- Management of Postoperative Urinary Retention
content: In general, patients with a history of significant preoperative urinary dysfunction or those with large volumes of urine drained (typically >1000-1500 mL) may benefit more from indwelling Foley catheterization, as this maximizes bladder muscle rest, rehabilitation, and recovery. [3] For most patients with POUR, intermittent self-catheterization 4 times daily is recommended when possible. [3] The University of Michigan, Ann Arbor, has published a practical algorithm to help clarify this issue. [84] Regardless of the initial treatment method chosen, patients should remain on alpha-blocker therapy until cleared by their clinician or urologist.

title: Postoperative Urinary Retention -- Treatment / Management -- Management of Postoperative Urinary Retention
content: An episode of urinary retention, whether postoperative or otherwise, should be regarded as an insult to the bladder, as animal models have demonstrated detrusor damage and impaired contractility. [48] However, these changes have proven to be reversible with continued bladder decompression. [85] On this basis, our institution favors the use of indwelling catheterization in the management of POUR.

title: Postoperative Urinary Retention -- Treatment / Management -- Management of Postoperative Urinary Retention
content: Regardless of the catheterization method, American Urological Association guidelines recommend initiating alpha-blockers, such as tamsulosin 0.8 mg or alfuzosin 10 mg daily, in patients not already receiving these agents before a voiding trial if normal micturition does not resume within a few hours following anesthesia. [86] Regarding medical treatment of POUR, medical alpha-blockade has demonstrated the most significant overall benefit in terms of risk-benefit analysis, followed by opioid antagonists, nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs, and cholinergic agonists. [81] [87] [88] [89] [90]

title: Postoperative Urinary Retention -- Treatment / Management -- Management of Postoperative Urinary Retention
content: Tamsulosin and afluzosin may begin to exert therapeutic effects within 4 to 8 hours, but clinically significant improvement generally requires about 3 to 5 days, with maximal benefit potentially taking several weeks. [91] [92] [93] The full dose of tamsulosin (0.8 mg daily) is typically initiated to facilitate voiding after an episode of urinary retention, and then later reduced to 0.4 mg daily if desired. Consequently, catheter removal or a voiding trial is typically recommended after 1 to 3 days of catheterization. [87]

title: Postoperative Urinary Retention -- Treatment / Management -- Management of Postoperative Urinary Retention
content: When an indwelling catheter is in place, there is no role for bladder training or periodically clamping/unclamping the catheter to retrain the bladder before Foley catheter removal. [3] [94] POUR alone is not an indication for hospitalization, as outcomes do not differ between patients who remain hospitalized before a voiding trial and those who go home and return later to the clinic for a voiding trial. [3] [95] If a patient then fails 1 or more voiding trials after 72 hours, or if there is suspicion of a more severe underlying voiding problem, an outpatient urological evaluation is recommended. [3] [96] Such evaluation may include cystoscopy, uroflowmetry, retrograde urethrography, and urodynamics. [3]

title: Postoperative Urinary Retention -- Differential Diagnosis
content: The differential diagnosis for a postoperative patient who has not urinated within a reasonable time frame includes: Acute kidney injury Ascites Bilateral iatrogenic ureteral obstruction Bladder perforation Cardiac failure Dehydration and hypovolemia (typically ruled out if a bladder scan demonstrates a full bladder) Hydronephrosis (bilateral) Iatrogenic bilateral ureteral injury or unilateral injury in a patient with a solitary kidney (typically ruled out if a bladder scan demonstrates a full bladder) Iatrogenic bladder injury (typically ruled out if a bladder scan demonstrates a full bladder) Kidney failure/shutdown Shock

title: Postoperative Urinary Retention -- Prognosis
content: As discussed, the development of POUR is multifactorial, involving pain, ambulation, medication, and other factors. POUR typically resolves after the removal/improvement of these modifiable inciting factors. Although acute retention can injure the detrusor muscle, drainage and bladder rest can reverse these changes. [48] [85] In most cases, bladder decompression, initiation of α-blocker therapy, and a tincture of time from the operation are sufficient. Most patients resume normal voiding function upon a trial without catheterization, 1 to 3 days from catheter placement. Two situations tend to oppose this trend—patients whose surgeries involved pelvic nerves vital to micturition and patients with severe, unidentified voiding problems preexisting before the surgery.

Factors associated with failure of a trial without catheterization include age older than 70, significant preexisting voiding symptoms, history of spinal surgery, hydronephrosis, and bladder volumes exceeding 1000 mL at the time of catheter insertion. [95] [97]

title: Postoperative Urinary Retention -- Pearls and Other Issues
content: The following points summarize key clinical pearls, common pitfalls, and important considerations in the management and prevention of POUR. POUR is a relatively common complication, with reported incidence ranging from 5% to 70% across studies. Patient characteristics leading to increased risk of POUR include older age, male sex, renal failure, diabetes mellitus, depression, benign prostatic hyperplasia, and higher American Urological Association or International Prostate Symptom Score. High-risk patients should receive preoperative or postoperative counseling regarding their increased risk of POUR. Prophylactic selective α-blocker therapy (eg, tamsulosin or alfuzosin) should be considered in high-risk patients who are not already receiving treatment for benign prostatic hyperplasia before surgery.

title: Postoperative Urinary Retention -- Pearls and Other Issues
content: Patients with unusually large urine volumes drained (often ≥1500 mL) may be at increased risk of postobstructive diuresis. [104] This condition is typically defined as the production of 200 mL or more of urine over at least 2 consecutive hours immediately following relief of urinary retention. [104] Additionally, it is defined as urinary excretion exceeding 3000 mL within 24 hours. [104] Please see StatPearls' companion resource, " Postobstructive Diuresis ," for further information. [104]

title: Postoperative Urinary Retention -- Pearls and Other Issues
content: The goal is to ensure that no urine volume is drained beyond the normal maximum bladder capacity of 500 mL. The timing should be adjusted accordingly. Patients should not be kept in the hospital solely to undergo a voiding trial, which can be performed as an outpatient. There is no evidence of any benefit from bladder training (where the Foley catheter is briefly clamped intermittently) before performing a voiding trial. Patients who fail an initial voiding trial need to have their Foley catheters replaced or learn intermittent self-catheterization. Another voiding trial can be scheduled in 1 to 2 weeks or as appropriate.

title: Postoperative Urinary Retention -- Enhancing Healthcare Team Outcomes
content: Acute urinary retention is a common postoperative complication and should be optimally managed by an interprofessional healthcare team. Effective diagnosis and management require coordinated efforts that include preventive measures, identification of high-risk patients, intraoperative and postoperative monitoring, and prompt treatment when recognized. Surgeons should identify patients preoperatively at high risk of developing POUR, educate them about their increased risk, and consider prescribing a preoperative prophylactic alpha-blocker, such as tamsulosin. Intraoperatively, the anesthesia team should keep in mind that POUR correlates with the volume of intravenous fluids given, and the surgeon should keep in mind that the duration of the operation and anesthesia are linked to the development of POUR.

title: Postoperative Urinary Retention -- Enhancing Healthcare Team Outcomes
content: Each anesthetic modality carries different risks of postoperative retention. Postoperatively, PACU and floor nurses should be aware that patients without a Foley catheter who fail to void within a reasonable time frame should be encouraged to void and, if possible, ambulate early. If a patient is unable to void after surgery, application of a suprapubic warm compress may help facilitate urination. Surgeons and hospitalists managing postoperative patients should keep in mind that opioids can increase the risk of POUR. Bedside ultrasonic bladder scanners should be used routinely to identify patients approaching potentially harmful bladder volumes (usually ≥450 mL) or who have failed to void within a reasonable time frame (6-8 h after last void or by 3 h after surgery).

title: Postoperative Urinary Retention -- Enhancing Healthcare Team Outcomes
content: If POUR develops, the bedside nurse should identify the condition and promptly notify the surgeon, hospitalist, or anesthesiologist. The managing clinician should then order either an indwelling or intermittent catheterization and initiate selective alpha-blockade with tamsulosin or alfuzosin. If pharmaceutical care is an option, the pharmacist should be involved by verifying dosing, performing medication reconciliation, and advising the team on potential adverse effects.

title: Postoperative Urinary Retention -- Enhancing Healthcare Team Outcomes
content: A trial without catheterization is typically performed within 1 to 3 days, based on the clinician's order or institutional protocol, and carried out by nursing staff. Following Foley removal, careful monitoring of voiding function is essential to prevent recurrent bladder overdistension. A postvoid residual volume of less than 200 mL is generally considered indicative of a successful voiding trial. If a patient fails the voiding trial, the Foley catheter should be replaced, or the patient should be taught to perform intermittent self-catheterization 4 times daily. Referral to urology for further outpatient evaluation and management is recommended. [3] [96] A coordinated interprofessional approach is critical to optimizing outcomes in patients with POUR.
